title: She Built Two AI Businesses Solo, Here's the exact System
description:
If you want to master frontier technical AI skills and become the AI-native builder and operator companies are desperately looking to hire, go here: https://agentfellow.ai/pfyt-vw7me

What happens when one person, with no team and no funding, builds a
multi-million dollar software business in public?

In this episode I sat down with Sabrina, founder of Blotato and previously co-founder of Qurious a real-time speech recognition company she sold to Pegasystems.

After that exit she was burnt out and had no intention of building again. She just wanted to teach people AI. But as her audience grew, she hit her own problem: repurposing one video across every platform was eating her week. She made a YouTube video showing her make.com workaround, and the comments all said the same thing, this is too hard, just build the app.

So she did. In public, on camera, from the first line of code.

She filmed the entire MVP build as a seven-part YouTube series. The first version couldn't even publish to social media — it was bolted to Zapier. Ten days after launch it was doing $10K MRR. Less than two years later, Blotato had crossed millions in ARR, and she hadn't hired anyone.

In this episode Sabrina walks through the whole thing, including the parts that went wrong: the waitlist program that cost her a month because what people said didn't match what they did, the launch newsletter that went to tens of thousands of subscribers with a dead video link, and the 30%+ churn in the first two months.

You'll see how a solo founder can:
→ Validate an idea with a 30-second unscripted TikTok before writing any code
→ Cut an MVP down to the one feature that actually needs to exist
→ Go from vibe coding to AI-assisted coding without shipping spaghetti to prod
→ Fix activation by watching session recordings instead of building dashboards
→ Know when to stop coding it yourself and hire a real developer
→ Pick a market by finding where people already pay for something worse
→ Build distribution from zero on the platform most generous to new creators
→ Use free Claude skills to write, grade and cross-post content on a loop
→ Run an entire content operation in one day a week

If you're a founder, product leader, or operator wondering whether you can build without a team, this episode is a step-by-step look at someone who did.

—

RESOURCES FROM SABRINA

Free Claude skills, content coach, brand brief, post writer, post grader, repurposing, viral hooks and cross-posting:
https://help.blotato.com/claude-skills/claude-skills

Her social media playbook, slightly outdated, but in her words covers
pretty much everything she did going from 0 to ~2M followers:
https://help.blotato.com/tips-and-tricks/sabrina-playbook

If you'd rather not set up the Claude skills, here's a standalone library
of hooks: https://help.blotato.com/tips-and-tricks/hooks

—

TIMESTAMPS

00:00  Intro
02:30  Qurious, real-time speech recognition, and the Pegasystems exit
05:49  Burnt out and not wanting to start another company
08:41  Validating the idea with a 30-second TikTok
11:18  Filming the MVP build in public
14:24  Cutting features until only one remained
16:06  The waitlist program that cost her a month
19:21  Launch day, and the link that didn't work
20:00  $10K MRR in ten days
22:27  Watching user sessions to fix onboarding
25:10  30% churn and why she wasn't worried
27:39  Vibe coding vs AI-assisted coding
30:44  Running a one-person AI-native business
32:35  How to choose a market worth entering
34:01  Building distribution from zero
36:23  What to actually post
38:20  Why you should copy the hook
40:26  The free Claude skills and hooks library
44:07  The cross-post skill
44:55  One day a week, start to finish
48:46  Videos edited entirely by AI
53:25  Bootstrapping vs fundraising
summary:
**00:00–06:30 | Demand before product.** Sabrina says her earlier real-time speech-recognition company Qurious sold to Pegasystems, after which she did not want another startup. Her growing AI-education audience exposed a personal problem: fragile Make.com workflows for repurposing one video across platforms. Comments asking for an app led to an unscripted TikTok validating the pain and one-to-one calls with roughly 10–20 commenters about their existing tools and spending; interest in a comment alone was not treated as proof of demand.

**06:30–14:15 | A deliberately incomplete MVP and an imperfect launch.** She filmed a seven-part build, stripped a multi-platform plan down to generating a Facebook post from pasted content, and used Zapier because the first app could not publish itself. An early-access cohort of about 50 people misled her: PostHog sessions contradicted their survey answers, and she says skipping that program could have saved about a month. At the October 20 launch, a newsletter sent to perhaps 50,000–70,000 people contained a dead demo-video link, yet she reports reaching $10,000 monthly recurring revenue about ten days later, helped by an existing audience and hundreds of waitlist signups. These are her account of her business, not independently audited figures.

**14:15–25:10 | Activation, code and a market wedge.** Watching user sessions revealed payment friction, rage clicks and an onboarding flow that dropped users into a blank interface; she switched to three explicit steps ending in draft posts. She estimates first-month-or-two churn above 30%, but kept improving activation because distribution brought a steady stream of new signups. She argues vibe coding should validate an idea and win the first 10–100 paying users before hiring an engineer; in her case she waited until millions in ARR, while personally reviewing architecture, tests and AI-generated changes because unattended changes had broken production. She favors an existing paid market—Buffer, Hootsuite and others in her example—where a product can excel on one dimension, rather than needing to replace every feature.

**25:10–39:55 | Distribution as a repeatable system.** She recommends TikTok for new creators: her first roughly 100,000-view post came after six weeks, following a move from daily posting to three times daily, though those are her own results. Basic ChatGPT lessons outperformed sophisticated agent lessons for her wider audience; she urges adapting proven hooks and post structures with one's own substance. Her free Claude skills include a brand brief, coach, writer, grader and roughly 100 hooks; her example loop revises a week's posts until they score nine out of ten, while a cross-post skill transcribes locally with Whisper, adjusts captions, waits for approval and schedules distribution. She shows AI-edited B-roll and tier-list videos, not proof that every output needs no review.

**39:55–46:12 | Working cadence and ownership.** She describes a former one-day-a-week batch: a YouTube recording and newsletter in the morning, then up to 20 short videos after lunch, with ideas gathered from her own AI sessions and trend scraping. She says content work expanded to two days a week when she added more long-form YouTube, while the business went from zero to millions in ARR before her first full-time hire. Her closing advice is to consider bootstrapping a $1–2 million-a-year solo software business instead of assuming a venture-scale exit is mandatory; profitable traction can leave a later fundraising option open. The chapter timestamps in the creator description do not match this caption timeline, so the library uses transcript-aligned topic shifts.
why_valuable: This helps a founder decide whether to test a narrow, paid content-automation problem with an audience-led MVP, and when to move from AI-prototyped code to engineered production software rather than fundraise or hire prematurely.
key_takeaways: 04:30–06:30: Sabrina tested the repurposing pain with a roughly 30-second TikTok, then interviewed about 10–20 commenters about tools and budgets; comments alone were not enough.
07:00–10:10: Her first version generated a Facebook post from pasted material and depended on Zapier for publishing; she reports this limited MVP still reached $10K MRR.
10:20–13:25: A roughly 50-person early-access program contradicted observed behavior and delayed launch, whereas a dead demo link in the October 20 newsletter did not prevent signups.
14:57–18:30: Session recordings and guided three-step onboarding addressed friction; she estimates churn initially exceeded 30% and cautions that distribution only buys time to improve retention.
19:07–22:10: She advocates AI-built MVPs for the first 10–100 paying users, then engineer-led architecture and QA; she reports AI changed unrelated production code when left unchecked.

25:29–33:59: Her own TikTok growth came from frequent raw posts aimed at basic AI needs, proven hooks, and iterative Claude post grading—not a claim that copying another creator’s substantive work is necessary.
34:59–41:35: Her cross-post workflow uses local Whisper, human approval and scheduled posts; she says one batch day covered early growth and later added a second day for long-form content.
43:46–45:55: Her verdict favors bootstrapped cash flow with the option to raise later, rather than a billion-dollar outcome as the only measure of success.

chapters.title: A problem emerging from an audience
chapters.description: After exiting Qurious to Pegasystems, Sabrina says she was burnt out and preferred teaching AI to founding again. As her audience grew, repurposing one video across channels became laborious; viewers of her Make.com workaround asked for a maintained app instead of another fragile automation.

chapters.title: Testing willingness to solve the problem
chapters.description: She posted an unscripted TikTok explaining a possible content-repurposing service and asked for feedback before writing code. She then called roughly 10–20 commenters to learn what tools they actually used and paid for, distinguishing a promising comment from a concrete workflow.

chapters.title: Seven public build episodes and a tiny first release
chapters.description: A seven-part series showed product planning, scope cuts, UI and authentication while she used Cursor to implement the first version. The release could turn pasted content into a Facebook post but used Zapier to publish; omitting a native publisher let her test demand before building a complete social suite.

chapters.title: The waitlist that obscured user behavior
chapters.description: Her early-adopter form produced about 50 selected participants with conflicting needs, and their observed PostHog sessions did not match their survey answers. She calls the cohort a mistake that cost weeks to a month and suggests launching earlier when self-reported use cases fail to converge.

chapters.title: A broken demo link and a fast revenue milestone
chapters.description: The October 20 launch newsletter included a link to a deleted demo video after a last-minute reupload; Sabrina estimates it went to 50,000–70,000 subscribers. People could still reach the website, and she reports $10,000 MRR roughly ten days later, explicitly tying that speed to existing trust and a large waitlist.

chapters.title: Watching recordings to repair activation
chapters.description: Instead of building elaborate analytics dashboards first, she spent hours watching PostHog sessions for rage clicks, sign-up trouble and people unsure where to start. She replaced an open-ended interface with a three-step path from source link to chosen platforms to draft posts, making initial value easier to reach.

chapters.title: Churn and the distinction between prototypes and production
chapters.description: She estimates churn exceeded 30% in the first month or two, but incoming signups let her iterate on activation and targeting. Her advice is to use vibe coding to validate and find 10–100 paying customers, then bring in a developer; her own AI-assisted workflow still requires architectural decisions, tests and review after production breakages.

chapters.title: A solo business with a focused competitive wedge
chapters.description: She says Blotato reached millions in annual recurring revenue before her first full-time hire, while warning that product and technical judgment still matter. To choose a market, she looks for people already paying competitors such as Buffer or Later and tries to win one important dimension rather than reproduce every competing feature.

chapters.title: From simple TikToks to tested hooks
chapters.description: She says TikTok rewarded her raw AI-teaching posts after about six weeks, and increasing to three daily posts coincided with stronger growth. Basic prompts appealed more widely than complex agents; she recommends borrowing effective opening structures and adding personal expertise because a technically strong post still needs to stop a viewer scrolling.

chapters.title: Skills, cross-posting and a batched content calendar
chapters.description: Her free Claude skills store a brand brief, draft and grade posts against a rubric, then revise the hook; a separate workflow transcribes a recorded video with local Whisper and waits for approval before scheduling adapted versions. She describes filming a long video and many shorts on one day each week, using accumulated ideas and AI-assisted video editing to protect time for building.

chapters.title: Bootstrapping preserves future choices
chapters.description: Asked about fundraising, she contrasts the pressure of venture-scale outcomes with the appeal of a cash-flowing solo software company earning one or two million dollars a year. Her argument is not that investment is forbidden: self-funded traction can create the option to raise later if the founder decides to pursue a larger company.

title: Keo & Zels: Boks lose but win big
description: The boys tip their hats to the wonderful Wallabies but remind despondent Bok fans that this season was about winning the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.
summary:
**00:00–08:20 | Credit Australia, diagnose Perth.** Keo and Zels congratulate the Wallabies on a 42–38 win and reject treating the late Springbok comeback as proof South Africa deserved victory. Keo says Australia had 62% possession and territory with the score still 17–17 around the 35th minute; he criticizes Rassie Erasmus for waiting until about the 47th minute to introduce a stronger bench, by which time Australia had built a 20-point lead. They disagree over whether four Australian yellow cards damaged the spectacle or were earned by South African scrum pressure, and criticize lengthy TMO interruptions. Their account is match analysis, not independently verified match statistics.

**08:20–20:05 | Rotation without combinations.** The hosts say 13 changes after the All Blacks series left a nominally deep Bok squad without the connections of its preferred XV, especially in the front row, lineout, midfield and aerial contest. They argue substitutes were being assessed unfairly in unfamiliar combinations against a settled Australian side; one example is a hooker they say has played 11 Tests with seven different front rows. A low kicking volume, heavy reliance on expansive passing, errors and intercept opportunities let the Wallabies dictate the game. Keo acknowledges fatigue after the demanding New Zealand series as a counterargument to starting more first-choice players.

**20:05–30:55 | How to play Australia and what the loss means.** Keo cites the Erasmus-era record as seven wins and six losses against Australia, including five losses in eight trips to Australia, and the pair say Australian width and tempo can lure the Boks away from their direct, set-piece-oriented strengths. Zels argues the team may eventually need a hybrid defense against attacks that get around the blitz; he also says Jacques Nienaber's absence removes a trusted pragmatic counterweight to Erasmus, clearly an opinion rather than an established causal fact. Both still regard winning three of four All Blacks Tests in the rivalry series as the season's priority and expect a more direct November approach.

**30:55–50:55 | World Cup depth versus knockout cohesion.** They debate when rotation should stop before the 2027 World Cup, naming unresolved backup roles at hooker, fullback and scrum-half while also recognizing progress from emerging players such as Ethan Hooker and Zachary Porthen. One host points out only three Perth starters and five match-day players had started or appeared in the 2023 World Cup final, respectively; his point is to resist treating the defeat as a direct test of the championship XV. Their practical conclusion is to introduce prospects into established units rather than change an entire lineup and style at once; Australia earned the win and may carry confidence into the Bledisloe series, but a single defeat does not erase the rivalry-series victory.

**50:55–59:20 | Four URC wins, with a caution.** The conversation shifts to wins for the Stormers, Lions, Sharks and Bulls in the United Rugby Championship's opening round, two home and two away. They praise comeback resilience and young players but worry that South African teams force spectacular offloads or cross-kicks instead of patiently building attacks near the opposition 22. The closing verdict is to give the Wallabies their due, keep perspective on the Boks and follow the club campaign rather than panic over one Test.
why_valuable: This helps a Bok supporter or selector judge whether the Perth loss reveals a systemic World Cup problem or a rotation-and-cohesion problem, and which backup roles and match tactics deserve closer scrutiny before 2027.
key_takeaways: 01:34–03:19: Keo says Australia were level 17–17 despite 62% possession and territory around 35 minutes, and argues introducing the bench only around minute 47 was too late; he credits Australia with a 42–38 win.

03:34–06:45: The hosts dispute the effect of four yellow cards: Zels dislikes reduced-player spectacles, while Keo says Bok pressure produced the cards and a comeback win would have concealed the earlier failures.
08:58–15:17: Thirteen starting changes produced weak combinations and exposed aerial, lineout and defensive alignment issues; fatigue after four All Blacks Tests is their explicit caveat.

15:56–23:16: Their tactical critique is that expansive play and limited kicking fed turnovers, while Australia excelled at moving the contest wide; they favor direct phases and set-piece pressure rather than matching the Wallabies’ pace.

20:25–26:55: Keo cites seven wins in 13 against Australia under the coaching regime and five away losses in eight; Zels’s argument that Nienaber would restrain Erasmus is stated as his view, not a proven explanation.

27:28–38:33: Winning three of four Tests against the All Blacks remains their seasonal benchmark, but they want decisions on backup hooker, fullback and scrum-half and a clearer end to whole-lineup experimentation.
45:28–49:21: They see progress among young Boks yet distinguish depth from a cohesive knockout XV; a prospect replacing one regular is not the same test as starting alongside 12 other changes.

51:13–59:20: All four South African URC sides won their first round, but the hosts warn that rushed red-zone offloads and kicks can squander dominance; they close by crediting Australia and rejecting panic.

chapters.title: Perth result and bench timing
chapters.description: The hosts concede the Wallabies deserved their 42–38 win, even though the Boks nearly came back after Australian yellow cards. Keo argues the game was already slipping away with the score level at 35 minutes and that the stronger bench arrived too late to control the momentum.

chapters.title: Cards, stoppages and a legitimate winner
chapters.description: Zels worries that four yellows turn a Test into an uneven spectacle, while Keo says repeated scrum pressure earned penalties and cards rather than merely benefiting from bad luck. Both dislike extended TMO interruptions, yet neither treats refereeing as a reason to deny Australia credit for its attacking performance.

chapters.title: Thirteen changes and an unfair audition
chapters.description: Rotating 13 starters meant backup players had to prove themselves without familiar front-row, lineout or midfield combinations against a more settled side. The hosts raise fatigue from the All Blacks series as a real constraint, but argue that introducing fewer prospects beside regular starters would better measure World Cup readiness.

chapters.title: Why abandoning the direct game hurt
chapters.description: The hosts cite limited kicking, lost territory and rushed passing as reasons Australia could exploit interceptions and broken play. They describe isolated good attacks alongside weak collective timing; the practical criticism is of trying to win an expansive game against an opponent especially skilled at it.

chapters.title: The Australian matchup and defensive questions
chapters.description: Keo highlights an uneven record on Australian soil, and Zels describes how Wallaby width can bait the Boks into playing faster and looser than they intend. They debate how opponents get around the blitz and whether a more varied defensive shape or a stronger pragmatic coaching voice is needed, without presenting that as a settled diagnosis.

chapters.title: Putting the defeat in the season’s context
chapters.description: Winning three of four Tests in the All Blacks rivalry series is, for both hosts, the larger accomplishment of the season. They expect Erasmus to take useful information from the Perth loss and to pursue a more direct style in November, although Zels wants the second-string players judged against the unusual circumstances of their selection.

chapters.title: How long should World Cup experimentation continue?
chapters.description: They argue over the risk of continuing large-scale rotation when a winning habit and clarity about backups matter before 2027. Zels identifies hooker, fullback and scrum-half as unresolved understudy spots; Keo counters that several first-choice roles are clearer than that picture suggests, even if elite starters cannot be replicated.

chapters.title: Wallaby strengths and Bok contenders
chapters.description: The Wallabies’ halfbacks, outside backs and aerial play earn detailed praise, but the hosts question their depth and front-row strength when injuries accumulate. They then name emerging Boks and returnees whose opportunities have improved their stock, while warning that depth only matters in a knockout when replacements can fit a coherent first team.

chapters.title: A clean URC sweep and the red-zone problem
chapters.description: The Stormers, Lions, Sharks and Bulls opened the URC with two away and two home wins, prompting praise for comebacks, young talent and strong kicking displays. The hosts also question impatient miracle passes and cross-kicks near the 22, suggesting more varied transition attacks rather than relying solely on set-piece entries.

chapters.title: Perspective after a mixed sporting weekend
chapters.description: Both presenters welcome four club victories while conceding the Springboks were the losing national side on a strong weekend for South African sport. They close by saluting the Australian result, keeping the rivalry-series triumph in perspective and turning attention to the coming URC and Champions Cup fixtures.

title: How to Use Grok Bot Better Than 99% of People (FULL COURSE)
channel: Brock Mesarich | AI for Non Techies
description:
✅ Use Higgsfield: https://higgsfield.ai/s/WByDQQ
✅ Connect Claude to 9,000+ Apps: https://bit.ly/4Ab7F42
✅ Blotato: https://www.blotato.com/?ref=brock
✅ Scrape with Firecrawl:  https://firecrawl.link/brock
✅ Use Granola: https://go.granola.ai/brock-mesarich
✅ ClickUp MCP: https://clickup.com/ 
🤖 Try Grok Bot: https://x.ai/bot
📚 Join my Skool Community for all of my resources: https://bit.ly/4t2yNgG

Most people who use Grok Bot are only scratching the surface, and this is the full course on squeezing everything out of it. In this video I walk through all 7 levels of Grok Bot, build my agents with you from scratch, and show you the one thing that turns a bunch of separate bots into an actual team. By the end you'll have AI agents doing real work for you while you're away.

0:00 - The full Grok Bot course
0:44 - Grok Bot vs Hermes Agent vs OpenClaw
4:25 - Level 1: Just message it
8:12 - Level 2: Plug in your tools
10:47 - Build a content agent with Higgsfield
15:33 - Turn a YouTube video into an Instagram carousel
18:44 - Auto-post it and wire the DM automation
22:15 - Firecrawl: live web context and the Deal Scout
25:14 - Level 3: Track every agent in ClickUp
32:22 - The meeting agent (Granola)
36:17 - Level 4: Routines
38:09 - One meeting note delegated to 5 agents
41:15 - Level 5: Memory and skills
42:01 - Zapier MCP: connect 9,000+ apps
45:53 - Level 6: Templates
48:05 - Level 7: Agent teams
49:49 - Wrap up
summary:
**00:00–08:12 | Who should use which agent.** Brock Mesarich argues Grok Bot is easier for non-technical users than Hermes Agent or OpenClaw because it is a hosted, mobile-friendly app with persistent agent conversations; he says self-hosted alternatives offer more model and workflow control. He presents his preference as a judgment, not a tested market share figure: his “90% of people” claim is an opinion. A health agent that remembers his usual breakfast and a 190-gram daily protein goal illustrates basic messaging before any integrations. His paid-plan and feature descriptions reflect what he saw at recording time, not independently confirmed current pricing.

**08:12–25:14 | From chat to a scheduled content-and-leads workflow.** He shows native plugins and MCP connections, adds Higgsfield to a specialist content bot, and gives it example carousels as style references. Feeding one of his own YouTube links yields a multi-slide carousel on the first attempt in about five or six minutes, which he judges usable; he distinguishes a previously successful 2,700-like carousel made with Claude Code from this new Grok Bot demonstration. He connects Blotato to schedule the new carousel and sets up a keyword-triggered Instagram DM carrying the video URL. Firecrawl is suggested for structured live web context and a price-alert “deal scout,” but the latter is described as a hypothetical use case rather than a completed end-to-end test.

**25:14–41:15 | Delegation with an observable task trail.** A separate tracker agent creates a three-column ClickUp board (to do, in progress, done) and instructs specialist bots to report starts, completions and blockers. In the demonstration, asking an Instagram bot to research a topic results in a visible in-progress ClickUp card. Next a Granola-connected meeting agent extracts action items from meeting notes, routes them to content, short-form, partnership and invoice bots, and is configured to sweep four times on weekdays; he shows a note being delegated to five agents and an invoice draft, not proof those outputs were externally completed. Routines can run by schedule or event.

**41:15–48:05 | Making workflows reusable and expanding integrations.** Brock recommends allowing memory to accumulate through repeated use and saving recurring procedures as skills rather than assuming a fresh bot knows the business. For apps not available natively he connects Zapier MCP and demonstrates reading his Drip campaign list; “9,000+ apps” refers to Zapier’s reported integration catalog, not a test of every connector. Template sharing can bundle instructions, skills, routines, files and integrations; he warns that a shared agent may expose confidential context or connected credentials, so inspect contents and permissions before publishing.

**48:05–50:10 | Specialist teams are the real payoff.** A chief-of-staff bot can hand tasks to operators, and he demonstrates two content bots discussing which owns the idea and posting schedule versus carousel visuals. His final recommendation is to build specialists with clear handoffs, connect only the needed apps, maintain a visible task board, and let the agents coordinate rather than fill one endless chat; the video shows selected examples, not a controlled reliability comparison against other agent platforms.
why_valuable: This helps a non-technical operator choose between a hosted agent and a self-hosted one and decide how to pilot a bounded content/meeting workflow with integrations, task visibility and credential checks before allowing autonomous publishing or invoicing.
key_takeaways: 00:44–04:25: Brock prefers hosted Grok Bot for ease of setup and mobile access; he acknowledges Hermes Agent gives developers more control and no harness fee, and his “90%” suitability estimate is opinion.

10:47–18:44: In his first-hand demo, Higgsfield and reference slides turn a YouTube video into a carousel in about five or six minutes; the older 2,700-like post he cites was created with Claude Code, not Grok Bot.
18:44–22:15: He shows Blotato scheduling the carousel and wiring a comment-keyword DM to a video link; scheduling and trigger setup are observed, not post-publication conversion results.
22:15–25:14: Firecrawl is proposed for structured live web input; the AirPods-below-$180 monitor is hypothetical, so no successful alert is demonstrated.
25:14–32:22: A ClickUp tracker with to-do/in-progress/done columns logs work by specialized agents; the demo shows an Instagram research job appear in progress after inter-agent messaging.

32:22–41:15: A Granola meeting-note agent routes action items to five agents and runs four weekday sweeps, but the transcript shows task dispatch and an invoice draft rather than confirmation of completed business outcomes.
42:01–48:05: Zapier MCP pulls a Drip campaign list and reportedly opens access to 9,000+ integrations; sharing templates requires checking included files, instructions and integration credentials.

48:05–50:10: His verdict is specialized agents with explicit task handoffs and a supervisor rather than one giant chat; two content agents negotiate responsibility for hooks versus slide visuals in his example.

chapters.title: A course built around agent specialization
chapters.description: Brock previews content, invoice and meeting agents working on separate tasks and coordinating with a chief-of-staff bot. He positions this as a progressive course rather than a benchmark; the examples later in the video provide the concrete evidence for his claims about autonomy.

chapters.title: Grok Bot vs Hermes Agent vs OpenClaw
chapters.description: He says a hosted app and phone messaging lower setup friction for beginners, whereas Hermes Agent and OpenClaw offer more customization, self-hosting and model choice. His recommendation for “90%” of users is personal judgment, and he notes hosted convenience also brings platform dependence and subscription cost.

chapters.title: Level 1: Just message it
chapters.description: Persistent threads behave like conversations with specialist teammates rather than isolated chats, illustrated by a health bot tracking meals and prompting him about a 190-gram protein target. He previews cross-agent messaging as the mechanism that later lets a chief-of-staff agent hand work to email and partnership specialists.

chapters.title: Level 2: Plug in your tools
chapters.description: Brock distinguishes native plugins from custom MCP connections and shows authorizing Google Drive in an existing set of 17 integrations. He uses these permissions to move agents beyond chatting into retrieval and actions across Gmail, calendar, ClickUp and creative tools; access scope should match the task.

chapters.title: Build a content agent with Higgsfield
chapters.description: He adds a creative-tool connection, creates a specialist rather than overloading his main bot, and defines its job in a plain-language brief. Reference carousel images specify cover typography, informative slides and a call to action, because an ungrounded image-generation prompt is less likely to match his brand.

chapters.title: Turn a YouTube video into an Instagram carousel
chapters.description: He supplies reference images and a link to his own five-use-cases video; the agent extracts topics and produces carousel slides after about five or six minutes. He likes the first result but the 2,700-like post he showed as a prior example came from Claude Code, not this Grok Bot run, so the engagement number is not an outcome of the demo.

chapters.title: Auto-post it and wire the DM automation
chapters.description: Using Blotato MCP, he schedules the generated carousel for 5 p.m. Pacific and checks the calendar, which displays a different local time. He then sets a Grok-comment trigger that sends a video link by DM; the demonstrated result is configuration, not verified future posting or lead conversion.

chapters.title: Firecrawl: live web context and the Deal Scout
chapters.description: He recommends Firecrawl to turn fresh web pages into structured context instead of relying only on model training or inefficient browsing. The AirPods-under-$180 alert is an illustrative price-watch proposal; the transcript does not show an actual alert firing, so it is a possible workflow rather than a completed test.

chapters.title: Level 3: Track every agent in ClickUp
chapters.description: A three-column board tracks to-do, in-progress and completed work with deadlines and agent names; a separate tracker bot instructs peers to report starts, completions and blockers. In his live example a carousel-research request appears as an in-progress task, creating an audit trail for delegation rather than relying on an agent’s claim that work happened.

chapters.title: The meeting agent (Granola)
chapters.description: Granola supplies meeting transcripts and extracted action items to a new meeting bot, which is tasked with routing work to specialist agents and updating ClickUp. Brock configures weekday note sweeps and later shows a single note generating tasks for content, outreach and invoices, but this alone cannot establish that every downstream action succeeded.

chapters.title: Level 4: Routines
chapters.description: He opens a weekday Granola sweep set for four daily checks and explains that routines can also use schedules or triggers such as new Slack messages. A test-run button can start a job outside its normal time, making repeatable work inspectable before leaving it unattended.

chapters.title: One meeting note delegated to 5 agents
chapters.description: A brain-dump note listing carousels, competitor research, partnership outreach and invoices is pulled into the meeting bot, which contacts five other agents. He inspects a competitor-research routine, carousel ideas and an invoice draft; the visible handoffs demonstrate routing, not that the email was actually sent or money collected.

chapters.title: Level 5: Memory and skills
chapters.description: He distinguishes accumulated context about his business from saved procedural instructions for a repeated workflow. Brock cautions that memory needs repeated use over days and recommends explicitly turning successful workflows into skills, rather than expecting a newly created agent to know every preference immediately.

chapters.title: Zapier MCP: connect 9,000+ apps
chapters.description: He uses Zapier as a bridge to Drip, an email-marketing app absent from his native plugin list, and shows the agent reading a campaign list. The 9,000-plus figure describes Zapier’s claimed app reach rather than connections personally tested, and he advises adding relevant apps and actions to the MCP server.

chapters.title: Level 6: Templates
chapters.description: He exports the carousel bot with skills and optional routines for a colleague and inspects instructions, files and integrations before publishing a share link. Because such exports can contain business context and potentially credential-bearing connections, the useful shortcut also requires reviewing what is being shared.

chapters.title: Level 7: Agent teams
chapters.description: Brock demonstrates a group conversation in which a short-form bot takes the hook, caption and posting schedule while a carousel bot owns visuals after the slide outline is ready. The explicit division of labor is his solution to overlapping bots, with a main agent coordinating specialists instead of manually repeating every handoff.

chapters.title: Wrap up
chapters.description: He closes by returning to seven levels from simple messaging through integrations, repeatable routines and coordinated teams. His verdict is that the hosted workflow is approachable for non-technical users, but the examples show setup and selected outputs rather than a measured reliability comparison with alternative agents.
